chunks: My father, may Allah grant him mercy, said: We were told by Sa'd bin Abdullah, from Ahmad bin Muhammad, from his father, from Hammad bin Isa, from some of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Complaining is not that a man says: 'I became ill yesterday' or 'I was ached yesterday'. However, complaining is that one says: 'I have become afflicted with what none has been afflicted with.'

key_terms.بِمَا لَمْ يُبْتَلْ بِهِ أَحَدٌ: With what no one else has been afflicted
key_terms.وَعَكْتُ: I was ached or suffered from a specific pain

ai.seo_question: What is the definition of true complaining (shakaya) in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In *Mani al-Akhbar*, Shaykh al-Saduq records Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishing between mundane reports of sickness and true *shakaya*, which implies a unique, existential burden or spiritual trial that sets one apart. This definition aligns with the Shia scholarly emphasis on *shukr* (gratitude) and *sabr* (patience), where complaining is discouraged unless it reflects a profound, singular test from God, thereby elevating the concept of suffering from a physical state to a spiritual station.

en.basel-kadem: 1.	My father, may Allah grant him mercy, said: We were told by Sa’d bin Abdullah, from Ahmad bin Muhammed, from his father, from Hammad bin Isa, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah, peace be upon him, that he said:
Complaining is not that a man says: «I became ill yesterday» or «I was ached yesterday». However, complaining is that one says: «I have become afflicted with what none has been afflicted with.»
